questions.q: In kishōtenketsu, what is the job of the ten?
choices: To introduce something unexpected, often seemingly unrelated
To mark the hero's lowest point
questions.explain: The ten is a turn or twist: a new element or angle. It needn't be a collision between opposing wills.

questions.q: Where did the four-part pattern originate?
choices: Classical Chinese poetry, as qǐ chéng zhuǎn hé
questions.explain: It began as a description of the four movements of a Chinese quatrain and spread to Japan and Korea.

questions.q: A four-panel comic: a cat stalks a bird; it creeps closer; cut to a vacuum cleaner switching on; the cat is now on top of the fridge. Which panel is the ketsu?
questions.explain: The last panel brings the unrelated twist and the setup together. That reconciliation is the ketsu.

questions.q: What's the most careful way to describe kishōtenketsu's relation to conflict?
choices: It is built around two opposing forces
Conflict can appear, but the structure doesn't need a central confrontation to drive it
It requires a villain in the third part
questions.explain: Stories using the pattern often contain conflict. What it doesn't require is a confrontation that everything revolves around.

questions.q: A columnist describes her garden, lingers on its routines, then turns to a war report, and closes by showing what links them. What structure is she using?
questions.explain: Introduction, development, an apparently unrelated turn, and a closing reconciliation.

questions.q: Which Western device is the closest cousin of the ten?
questions.explain: The volta is a turn in thought or perspective within a poem, much like the ten.

questions.q: Why do many writers find kishōtenketsu harder to use than it looks?
choices: It needs at least five acts
The ending must make the twist feel inevitable, or the piece reads as random
questions.explain: Everything rides on the ketsu connecting the twist to what came before.

ideas: A story can turn on a new perspective or an unrelated element rather than on a clash of wills.
The third of four movements introduces something that seems not to belong, and the fourth shows why it does.
The same four-part shape organizes a Chinese quatrain, a school essay and a newspaper comic strip.
